text: The Alps 2 Ocean Cycle Trail
A

New Zealand's Alps 2 Ocean Cycle Trail is a 301-kilometre cycling trail that goes from the foot of the Southern Alps to a town called Oamaru on the east coast. People can ride on a path that's made especially for bicycles, so they don't have to ride on the road or on footpaths. The trail features a mix of smooth paving, dirt tracks, and gravel areas. There are also small parts that are still on open roads, but those sections are becoming shorter as the trail continues to be developed. One of the best things about the Alps 2 Ocean is the relative ease of it and it is possible to ride the trail even if you're not in peak physical condition. There are no steep, long uphill climbs or very rough or technical sections and this allows riders of varying abilities, from beginners to experts, to enjoy the trail.

text: B

There are lots of things to see and explore along the way including wetlands and clay cliffs. The views from the trail are dramatic: beech forests, stretches of open plain, deep blue lakes and all the shades of golden brown from the hills, mountains and grasses. There are eight sections on the trail, and it can take from four days to just over a week to get through all eight of them. It really depends on the rider's fitness levels and how much they want to do around the trail.

text: C

The concept of a cycleway from the mountains to the sea came from farm manager Rick Ramsay. When he was driving his truck, he would see cyclists trying to avoid the highway, instead taking the safer and quieter route along the canals. He also drove regularly from his home to Oamaru, and would often take different routes to relieve the boredom of the trip. He thought of all the other beautiful back-country routes cyclists could take to head down to Oamaru instead of just cycling down the highway. When he was asked to chair a meeting called by the Tourism and Development Board, he introduced the idea of a trail from the mountains to the sea.

text: D

A committee was set up to develop the cycle way and apply for funding from the government. Then a plan was submitted and an agreement signed. Construction of the trail began in January 2011 and by the end of 2013, the trail was fully signposted and open to cyclists. Jason Gaskill, Tourism Board general manager, says it has been great to see this project come to life. However, to develop a project of this size inevitably means a few challenges along the way. At the beginning there was very little technical data available to assist with developing the trail, and there wasn't a lot of research available on cycle safety or on cycle tourism. Mr Gaskill says the only real low point, from his perspective, is the time it has taken to get some sections completed, as each section of the trail presented its own difficulties. For example, building around a large lake proved testing and careful management of native wetlands was necessary. Fortunately, the people involved had a great deal of expertise in this area. Another issue was that construction near Oamaru went close to private farm buildings which required negotiations with those that lived there.

text: E

Even though the trail welcomes thousands of people a year, further development continues. Work is going to be carried out on several new sections of trail to take cyclists off all roads that have a high speed limit. This will provide a safer riding experience, connecting existing trail sections and restricting cyclists' use of public roads to towns and urban areas. Further work is planned to better incorporate other townships and provide a more scenic riding experience. Minimising accidents and risk is a priority. and the public have communicated that they want more off-road trails so they are separated from traffic.

text: F

More support services have developed as a result of the growing number of cyclists in the area. One of these takes the form of organised tours with a knowledgeable guide who can give information about the area on the way. The relationship between businesses in the area and the developers of the trail has boosted the economy and produced a better overall riding experience. For example, riders can carry their own luggage or have it delivered to their accommodation, which means you don't have to carry the extra weight on your bike. Staff at the tourist information office on the Alps 2 Ocean Cycle Trail can provide all cyclists with a complimentary map so they don't need to buy one. This includes lots of information about all sorts of different aspects of the trail. Bikes are available for hire at the tourist information office and an additional service has just been set up whereby staff can now provide riders with clothing they might need on the trip for a small fee. If you go online, there are also regular updates about the weather for each section of the trail, which is important as it is quite changeable in this part of the country
